title: Part 2, Chapter 65
paragraphs: In which is made known who the Knight of the White Moon was; together with Don Gregorio's release, and other events

Don Antonio Moreno followed the Knight of the White Moon, and a number of boys followed him too — nay, pursued him — until they had him safely housed in a hostel in the heart of the city. Don Antonio, eager to make his acquaintance, went in too. A squire came out to meet him and remove his armour, and he shut himself into a lower room, still accompanied by Don Antonio, whose bread would not bake until he had found out who he was. The Knight of the White Moon, seeing that the gentleman would not leave him, said, "I know very well, señor, what you have come for: to find out who I am; and since there is no reason why I should conceal it from you, while my servant here is taking off my armour I will tell you the true state of the case, leaving nothing out. You must know, señor, that I am called the bachelor Samson Carrasco. I am from the same village as Don Quixote of La Mancha, whose craze and folly make all of us who know him feel pity for him — and I am one of those who have felt it most. Persuaded that his chance of recovery lay in quiet and in staying at home, I hit upon a scheme for keeping him there. Three months ago, therefore, I went out to meet him as a knight-errant under the assumed name of the Knight of the Mirrors, intending to engage him in combat and overcome him without hurting him, making it the condition of our combat that the loser should be at the victor's disposal. What I meant to demand of him (for I considered him already vanquished) was that he should return to his own village and not leave it for a whole year, by which time he might be cured. But fate ordered it otherwise: he defeated me and unhorsed me, and so my plan failed. He went on his way and I came back conquered, covered with shame, and badly bruised from my fall, which was particularly dangerous. But this did not quench my desire to meet him again and overcome him, as you have seen today. And since he is so scrupulous in observing the laws of knight-errantry, he will no doubt, in order to keep his word, obey the injunction I have laid on him. That, señor, is how the matter stands, and I have nothing more to tell you. I implore you not to betray me, or tell Don Quixote who I am; so that my honest efforts may succeed, and a man of excellent wits — were he only rid of the fooleries of chivalry — may get them back again."

"Oh señor," said Don Antonio, "may God forgive you the wrong you have done the whole world in trying to bring the most amusing madman in it back to his senses. Don't you see, señor, that the gain by Don Quixote's sanity can never equal the enjoyment his crazes give? But my belief is that all the señor bachelor's pains will be of no use in bringing a man so hopelessly cracked back to his senses; and if it weren't uncharitable, I would say may Don Quixote never be cured, for by his recovery we lose not only his own drolleries but his squire Sancho Panza's too — any one of which is enough to turn melancholy itself into merriment. However, I'll hold my peace and say nothing to him, and we'll see whether I am right in my suspicion that Señor Carrasco's efforts will be fruitless."

The bachelor replied that at any rate the affair was looking up, and he hoped for a happy result; and putting his services at Don Antonio's command, he took his leave. Having had his armour packed at once onto a mule, he rode away from the city that same day on the horse he had ridden into battle, and returned to his own country without any adventure worth recording in this truthful history.

Don Antonio reported to the viceroy what Carrasco had told him, and the viceroy was not very pleased to hear it, for with Don Quixote's retirement, the amusement of everyone who knew anything of his mad doings was at an end.

For six days Don Quixote kept to his bed, dejected, melancholy, moody and out of sorts, brooding over the unhappy event of his defeat. Sancho tried to comfort him, and among other things said to him, "Hold up your head, señor, and be of good cheer if you can, and give thanks to heaven that if you've had a tumble to the ground you haven't come off with a broken rib; and, as you know, 'where they give they take,' and 'there are not always fletches where there are pegs,' a fig for the doctor — there's no need of him to cure this ailment. Let's go home, and give up wandering about in search of adventures in strange lands and places. Properly looked at, I'm the greater loser, though it's your worship that has had the worse usage. With the government I gave up all wish to be a governor again, but I did not give up all longing to be a count — and that will never come to pass if your worship gives up becoming a king by renouncing the calling of chivalry; and so my hopes are going to turn into smoke."

"Peace, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "you see that my suspension and retirement are not to exceed a year. I shall soon return to my honoured calling, and I shall not be at a loss for a kingdom to win and a county to bestow on you."
"May God hear it and sin be deaf," said Sancho; "I have always heard say that 'a good hope is better than a bad holding.'"

As they were talking, Don Antonio came in looking extremely pleased and exclaiming, "Reward me for my good news, Señor Don Quixote! Don Gregorio and the renegade who went for him have come ashore — ashore do I say? They are by this time at the viceroy's house, and will be here in a moment."

Don Quixote cheered up a little and said, "Truly, I am almost ready to say I should have been glad if it had turned out just the other way, for it would have obliged me to cross over to Barbary, where by the might of my arm I should have restored to liberty not only Don Gregorio but all the Christian captives there are in Barbary. But what am I saying, miserable creature that I am? Am I not the one who has been defeated? Am I not he who has been overthrown? Am I not he who must not take up arms for a year? Then why am I making professions? What am I bragging about, when it is fitter for me to handle the distaff than the sword?"

"No more of that, señor," said Sancho; "'let the hen live, even if it be with her pip;' 'today for you and tomorrow for me;' in these matters of encounters and whacks one mustn't mind them, for he who falls today may get up tomorrow — unless he chooses to lie in bed, I mean gives in to weakness and doesn't pluck up fresh spirit for fresh battles. Let your worship get up now and receive Don Gregorio; the household seems to be in a bustle, and no doubt he's here by now." And so it proved, for as soon as Don Gregorio and the renegade had given the viceroy an account of the voyage out and home, Don Gregorio, eager to see Ana Felix, came with the renegade to Don Antonio's house. When they carried him off from Algiers he was in woman's dress; on board the vessel, however, he had exchanged it for that of a captive who escaped with him. But whatever dress he wore he looked like one to be loved and served and admired, for he was strikingly handsome, and to judge by appearances about seventeen or eighteen years old. Ricote and his daughter came out to welcome him — the father with tears, the daughter with bashfulness. They did not embrace, for where there is deep love there will never be overmuch boldness. Seen side by side, the handsomeness of Don Gregorio and the beauty of Ana Felix were the wonder of everyone present. It was silence that spoke for the lovers at that moment, and their eyes were the tongues that declared their pure and happy feelings. The renegade explained the measures and means he had used to rescue Don Gregorio, and Don Gregorio, at no great length but in a few words that showed his intelligence ran ahead of his years, described the peril and embarrassment he had found himself in among the women he had been staying with. In short, Ricote liberally rewarded both the renegade and the men who had rowed; and the renegade effected his readmission into the Church and was reconciled with it — from a rotten limb becoming, by penance and repentance, a clean and sound one.

Two days later the viceroy discussed with Don Antonio the steps they should take to enable Ana Felix and her father to stay in Spain, for it seemed to them there could be no objection to a daughter who was so good a Christian and a father so well disposed in appearance remaining there. Don Antonio offered to arrange the matter at the capital, where he was compelled to go on some other business, hinting that many a difficult affair was settled there with the help of favour and bribes.

"No," said Ricote, who was present during the conversation, "it will not do to rely on favour or bribes, because with the great Don Bernardino de Velasco, Conde de Salazar, to whom his Majesty has entrusted our expulsion, neither pleas nor promises, bribes nor appeals to compassion, are of any use. Though it is true he mixes mercy with justice, still, seeing that the whole body of our nation is tainted and corrupt, he applies to it the cautery that burns rather than the salve that soothes. Through prudence, sagacity, care, and the fear he inspires, he has borne on his mighty shoulders the weight of this great policy and carried it into effect, all our schemes and plots, importunities and wiles, being useless to blind his Argus eyes, ever on the watch lest one of us should remain behind in concealment — and like a hidden root, in time, sprout and bear poisonous fruit in a Spain now cleansed and relieved of the fear in which our vast numbers held it. A heroic resolve on the part of the great Philip the Third, and unparalleled wisdom to have entrusted it to the said Don Bernardino de Velasco!"

"At any rate," said Don Antonio, "when I am there I will make every possible effort, and let heaven do as pleases it best. Don Gregorio will come with me to relieve the anxiety his parents must be suffering over his absence; Ana Felix will stay in my house with my wife, or in a monastery; and I know the viceroy will be glad that the worthy Ricote should stay with him until we see what terms I can make."

The viceroy agreed to all that was proposed; but Don Gregorio, on learning what had been arranged, declared he could not and would not on any account leave Ana Felix. However, since it was his purpose to go and see his parents and devise some way of returning for her, he fell in with the proposed arrangement. Ana Felix stayed with Don Antonio's wife, and Ricote in the viceroy's house.

The day for Don Antonio's departure came; and two days later that for Don Quixote's and Sancho's, since Don Quixote's fall did not let him take the road sooner. There were tears and sighs, swoonings and sobs, at the parting between Don Gregorio and Ana Felix. Ricote offered Don Gregorio a thousand crowns if he would have them, but he would not take any save five, which Don Antonio lent him and he promised to repay at the capital. So the two of them took their departure, and Don Quixote and Sancho afterwards, as has already been said — Don Quixote without his armour and in travelling gear, and Sancho on foot, Dapple being loaded with the armour.
